newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican VAT cuts could rattle markets -- business.
newsitem.headline: Mexican VAT cuts could rattle markets -- business.

text.p: Mexico's top business leader on Tuesday warned that a cut in value added tax proposed by opposition parties could unsettle the country's financial markets.

"A cut in VAT for us would mean a fiscal deficit of more than one percent, and that could lead to a spate of nervousness in the markets because there would be no way to finance that deficit," Eduardo Bours, head of the powerful Business Coordinating Council, told reporters.

His voice was added to a chorus of business leaders broadly opposing the tax cut, that opposition parties pledged in the run-up to July 6 elections and have since vowed to promote following their unprecedented success at the polls.

They say they are in agreement on cutting VAT to 10 percent from its current 15 percent level, though there is disagreement on how quickly the tax cut should take full effect, or how it should be paid for.

In the elections, the four main opposition parties won enough seats in the lower house of Congress to defeat the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) if it chooses to block the tax cut. During Mexico's peso crisis in 1995, the PRI voted almost unanimously to raise VAT to 15 percent.
But the PRI still retains control of the Senate, and could block any tax cuts there.
Bours said the private sector favored a broad fiscal reform package, and was in negotiations with the Finance Ministry on the issue. But he stressed he remained wedded to balanced budgets.
"A cut in VAT cannot solve our problems. What we need, I reiterate, is healthy policies (and)...a fiscal balance."

Leaders of Mexico's main pro-government labor union, the Mexican Workers Confederation, have also opposed the VAT cut, and the Finance Ministry says it would lead to higher debt levels in Mexico because it would cut reveunes by some 20 billion pesos.
